x: Option B is the incorrect statement: the Ninth Schedule, though created by the 1st Amendment, 1951 (Art. 31B) to shield land-reform laws, later grew to over 280 entries and did not stay confined to land reforms. Options A, C and D are correct statements.

Pairs 1, 2 and 4 are correct: Articles 25 and 28 are available to all persons, and Article 26 to religious denominations or any section of them. Pair 3 is wrong because Article 27 is also available to all persons (citizens and foreigners), not to citizens only.

D is the answer: Article 226 lets High Courts issue writs for Fundamental Rights and for 'any other purpose', so their subject-matter scope is wider, while Article 32 is confined to Fundamental Rights. A reverses this and B is wrong. C states a true fact (the Supreme Court is wider in territory, covering the whole of India), but D gives the full scope comparison the question asks for.

In Champakam Dorairajan (1951) the Supreme Court struck down a Madras communal order on admissions for violating Article 29(2). The First Amendment, 1951 responded by inserting Article 15(4), enabling special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes, SCs and STs.

The right to vote rests on adult suffrage under Article 326 and on statutory provisions (Section 62 of the RPA, 1951; registration under Section 19 of the RPA, 1950). B, C and D are wrong: the right to work is Article 41 (DPSP), information is part of Article 19(1)(a), and education for 6-14 is the Fundamental Right under Article 21A, not Article 45.
